text:
For the same 32 sampled negatives, balanced BCE gives gradients ∂L/∂s+=σ(s+)−1 and ∂L/∂sj=σ(sj)/32. Restricted softmax CE gives (p+−1)/τ and pj/τ, where p=softmax(s/τ). Derived from the documented [BCE](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss.html) and [CE](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss.html) definitions: at zero logits, τ=1, CE gradients are 64/33≈1.94 times BCE gradients. Away from initialization, no constant scaling equates them: CE couples all candidates and emphasizes relatively strong negatives; BCE treats each logit independently. If “identical negatives” means 32 copies of one item, BCE equals its one-negative version, while CE becomes softplus((s−−s+)/τ+log 32).

CE is invariant to adding a common offset to every candidate score; BCE anchors scores around zero. Both respond to score scaling. Temperature changes CE’s gradient magnitude and relative negative weighting, so learning-rate adjustment cannot reproduce it; [Wang and Liu](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.09740) analyze this hardness sensitivity. Neither loss inherently bounds embedding norms on separable data. BCE’s absolute-score anchoring is not weight regularization; dropout, weight decay, norm constraints, and early stopping remain separate factors.

Use paired initialization, batches, negative draws, architecture, reductions, regularization, and training budgets. Compare the objectives at τ=1, then add a constant-rescaled CE control and record gradient norms, actual optimizer updates, clipping frequency, and score distributions. Adam can largely cancel constant gradient scaling, complicating learning-rate equivalence. A small, equally budgeted learning-rate sweep for both objectives plus a CE temperature check is justified. Keep weight-decay semantics explicit. Select using macro validation HR@10 only; a fixed-hyperparameter result establishes performance under that configuration, not an isolated benefit from objective coupling.
